title: Reading a REIT: occupancy, WALE, yield and NAV
concept: Occupancy shows how much of the space is let out. Falling occupancy means falling rent.
WALE (weighted average lease expiry) shows how long, on average, tenants are committed to stay. A longer WALE gives more predictable income.
Distribution yield is the annual distribution divided by the current unit price. It is a rate on the price you pay today, not a return guarantee.
NAV (net asset value) is the value of the trust's assets less debt, per unit. Units can trade above or below NAV.
Check debt too: how much is borrowed against the assets, and when the loans must be repaid or refinanced.

client.quote: "This REIT shows a 7% yield. Is that my return?"
client.context: Client compares a REIT's yield with a bank fixed deposit.

talk: "The yield is the cash paid out divided by today's price. It can change if rent, occupancy or the unit price changes. Your total return also includes what happens to the unit price. A fixed deposit's rate is fixed. This is not."
remember: Long WALE, high occupancy = steadier income.
Price can be above or below NAV.

qs.prompt: A REIT paid ₹8 per unit in a year and the unit trades at ₹100. What is the distribution yield?
qs.why: Yield = annual distribution ÷ current price = 8 ÷ 100 = 8%. It can change if either number changes.

qs.prompt: What does a longer WALE usually indicate?
options: Tenants are committed for longer, so rental income is more predictable
qs.why: A longer weighted average lease expiry means leases run further out, reducing near-term vacancy risk. It guarantees nothing.

qs.prompt: Why can a REIT unit trade at a price different from its NAV?
options: Because the market prices future income, interest rates and sentiment, not just the book value
Because NAV is set by SEBI each day
Because REIT units cannot be sold
Because the trustee sets the price
qs.why: Like any listed security, a unit's price reflects demand and expectations. NAV is only one reference point.

title: The five listed REITs in India
concept: India has five listed REITs: Embassy Office Parks REIT, Mindspace Business Parks REIT, Brookfield India Real Estate Trust, Nexus Select Trust and Knowledge Realty Trust.
Most hold office parks and business parks. Nexus Select Trust holds retail malls.
Together, the five distributed more than ₹8,900 crore to unitholders in FY2026, to over 4.25 lakh unitholders (Indian REITs Association data as reported in May 2026).
Their combined portfolio is more than 187 million sq ft. Gross asset value was over ₹2.72 lakh crore in March 2026.
Each REIT differs in tenants, cities, lease profile and debt. Read the latest investor presentation, not just the yield.

client.quote: "Which REIT is the best one to buy?"
client.context: Client has ₹5 lakh and wants you to pick one name.

talk: "They own different kinds of buildings in different cities with different tenants and debt. There is no single best name. Let's look at occupancy, lease expiry, debt and how much of the portfolio each tenant makes up, and see which fits your plan."
remember: Mostly office; Nexus Select is malls.
Compare tenants, WALE, debt, not only yield.

qs.prompt: How many REITs are listed in India (as of mid-2026)?
qs.why: Embassy, Mindspace, Brookfield India, Nexus Select and Knowledge Realty Trust.

qs.prompt: Which listed REIT is built mainly around retail malls?
qs.why: Nexus Select Trust owns shopping malls. The others are mostly office and business parks.

qs.prompt: A client asks which REIT is best. What is the best first response?
options: Compare occupancy, lease expiry, debt and tenant concentration against the client's goals
Pick the one with the highest yield
Pick the one with the lowest unit price
qs.why: Yield alone ignores risk. Quality and fit come from the portfolio, leases and balance sheet.

title: Distributions and tax: what the cash payout is made of
concept: A REIT's payout can include interest, dividend, rental income and repayment of debt (return of capital). Each part can be taxed differently.
For resident investors, interest, dividend and rent components are generally taxed at slab rates in the unitholder's hands. Check the REIT's component-wise statement.
The return of capital part is not income in the usual sense, but it affects the cost of your units and therefore your gain or loss on sale.
On sale of listed units, gains up to 12 months are short-term (20%). Beyond 12 months they are long-term (12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption). Confirm current rules with a tax adviser.
Because the payout is a mix, the yield printed on a website is a pre-tax and pre-component number.

client.quote: "Is the REIT income tax free like my PPF?"
client.context: Client in the 30% slab compares REIT income with PPF interest.

talk: "No. Part of the payout can be taxed at your slab rate, and gains on selling the units are taxed too. The REIT sends a statement that splits the payout into parts. Let's look at the after-tax yield for your slab, and confirm the details with your CA."
remember: Payout = interest + dividend + rent + return of capital.

qs.prompt: Why is a REIT's headline yield not the same as what a taxpayer keeps?
options: The payout is made of parts that can be taxed at different rates, so yield before tax overstates the take-home amount
Because the REIT keeps part of the yield
Because yield is always taxed at 5%
Because REIT income is exempt for individuals
qs.why: The payout is a mix of income types. Taxes reduce the take-home return, especially for higher slabs.

qs.prompt: What is the 'return of capital' part of a distribution?
options: A portion that is a repayment rather than income, which affects the cost of the units
qs.why: It is treated differently from income and can reduce the cost of acquisition, changing the gain on sale. Confirm treatment with a CA.

qs.prompt: For listed REIT units held for more than 12 months, which long-term capital gains rate is currently quoted (above the ₹1.25 lakh exemption)?
qs.why: Listed units held beyond 12 months attract 12.5% LTCG above the exemption, under current rules. Rules can change; confirm before advising.

title: What an InvIT is: owning roads, power lines and pipelines
concept: An InvIT (Infrastructure Investment Trust) works like a REIT, but owns infrastructure such as toll roads, power transmission lines and pipelines.
Revenue comes from tolls, annuities from authorities, or tariffs. These depend on contracts, traffic and regulation.
Units are listed. Examples of Indian InvITs include IndiGrid, PowerGrid InvIT, IRB InvIT and Cube Highways Trust.
At least 90% of net distributable cash flows must be distributed, at least every six months for listed InvITs.
Infrastructure assets have long lives but can lose value as concessions run down. Check how many years of contract remain.

client.quote: "I want regular income. A friend suggested an InvIT that owns highways. Is it like a REIT?"
client.context: Retired client looking for monthly-ish income, low risk appetite.

talk: "An InvIT is similar in structure, but the assets are things like roads and power lines. Income depends on tolls or contracts. It is market-linked. If you need money you can count on, an InvIT should not be the main source."

qs.prompt: What does an InvIT typically own?
options: Infrastructure assets such as roads, power transmission and pipelines
qs.why: InvITs pool infrastructure projects and pass cash flows to unitholders.

qs.prompt: Which factor most directly affects a toll-road InvIT's income?
options: Traffic and the terms of the concession
qs.why: Toll revenue depends on traffic volumes and contract terms. Concession length limits how long the income runs.

qs.prompt: Which of these is an Indian listed InvIT?
qs.why: IndiGrid is an InvIT. The other three are REITs.

title: REIT versus InvIT: what differs and what does not
concept: Same idea: a SEBI-regulated trust, listed units, at least 90% of NDCF paid out, at least every six months.
Different assets: REITs hold rent-earning real estate; InvITs hold infrastructure projects.
Different income drivers: REIT income depends on occupancy and lease renewals; InvIT income depends on traffic, tariffs and contract terms.
At least 80% of a REIT's assets must be completed and rent-generating. InvITs have a similar completed-asset requirement.
From 1 January 2026, SEBI treats REITs as equity-related instruments for mutual funds. InvITs stay classified as hybrid.

client.quote: "What is the difference between a REIT and an InvIT? They sound the same."
client.context: Client has heard both terms from an online influencer.

talk: "Both are trusts that pay out most of their cash. A REIT owns buildings and earns rent. An InvIT owns roads, power lines or pipelines and earns tolls or tariffs. The risks are different, so I'd look at each separately."
remember: Same rules of payout, different assets.
Mutual funds: REIT equity-related, InvIT hybrid.

qs.prompt: What is the main difference between a REIT and an InvIT?
options: The type of assets they own: real estate for REITs, infrastructure for InvITs
REITs are unlisted and InvITs are listed
REITs guarantee returns and InvITs do not
One is regulated by SEBI and the other is not
qs.why: Both are SEBI-regulated listed trusts. The assets and what drives income differ.

qs.prompt: What minimum share of net distributable cash flows must both REITs and InvITs distribute?
qs.why: The 90% NDCF payout requirement applies to both structures.

qs.prompt: How are REITs and InvITs classified for mutual funds from 1 January 2026?
options: REITs as equity-related instruments; InvITs remain hybrid
REITs as hybrid; InvITs as equity
qs.why: SEBI's November 2025 circular reclassified REITs as equity-related from 1 January 2026. InvITs stay hybrid.

title: Risks: what can go wrong with REITs and InvITs
concept: Price risk: units trade on exchanges and can fall sharply in weak markets or when interest rates rise.
Interest rate risk: higher rates raise borrowing costs and make fixed-income alternatives more attractive, which can pressure unit prices.
Asset risk: lower occupancy, tenant exits, falling traffic or contract problems reduce income.
Leverage risk: heavy borrowing makes payouts more sensitive to refinancing costs. Leverage is capped at 49% of asset value, with limits on how it can be used.
Liquidity and concentration: some units trade thinly, and a few tenants or assets can make up a large share of income.

client.quote: "What is the worst that can happen?"
client.context: Cautious client who read headlines about falling office demand.

talk: "Unit prices can fall, payouts can be cut if rent or traffic drops, and borrowing costs matter. None of that is guaranteed to happen, and none of it is guaranteed not to. That is why we size it as a small part of your portfolio."
remember: Price, rate, asset, leverage, liquidity risks.

qs.prompt: Which event most directly reduces a REIT's distributable income?
options: A rise in the client's tax slab
A change in the fund manager of a mutual fund
qs.why: Rent is the REIT's income. Lower occupancy or rent lowers cash flow and distributions.

qs.prompt: Why can rising interest rates hurt REIT and InvIT unit prices?
options: Higher rates increase borrowing costs and make safer alternatives more attractive
Because the trust must repay all debt immediately
qs.why: Rate rises can hit both costs and relative attractiveness, pushing unit prices lower.

qs.prompt: What does the 49% leverage cap on REITs mean?
options: Borrowings are limited to 49% of asset value
The REIT must hold 49% in cash
Only 49% of rent can be distributed
49% of units must be held by the sponsor
qs.why: Debt is capped relative to asset value. It limits, but does not remove, leverage risk.

title: Where mutual funds fit: the 2026 reclassification
concept: From 1 January 2026, SEBI treats REITs as equity-related instruments for mutual funds and specialised investment funds (SIFs). InvITs remain hybrid.
Debt schemes that held REIT units on 31 December 2025 may keep them. AMCs are encouraged, not forced, to reduce REIT exposure in debt schemes over time.
REITs can be included in equity indices after a six-month buffer, meaning from July 2026 onwards. AMFI must place REITs into large-, mid- and small-cap lists.
Fund factsheets may now show REIT or InvIT units in equity or hybrid holdings. Read the holdings table and the scheme addendum.
A mutual fund holding REIT units is not the same as owning a REIT directly: you also pay the fund's expenses and take the fund manager's decisions.

client.quote: "My fund factsheet suddenly shows a REIT in the equity portfolio. Did the fund change?"
client.context: Client reads her statements closely and noticed new names.

talk: "SEBI changed how REITs are classified for mutual funds from January 2026, so they now count as equity-related. Your fund may hold them as one of many holdings. Let's check how much of the portfolio it is."
remember: REITs equity-related for MFs from 1 Jan 2026.

qs.prompt: From 1 January 2026, how does SEBI classify REITs for mutual funds?
qs.why: The 28 November 2025 circular made REITs equity-related for MFs and SIFs from 1 January 2026.

qs.prompt: What happens to REIT units held by debt schemes on 31 December 2025?
options: They must be sold within a week
qs.why: Grandfathering lets debt schemes keep existing REIT units; AMCs are encouraged to reduce exposure gradually.

qs.prompt: A client's equity fund shows a REIT among its holdings. What is the best explanation?
options: REITs now count as equity-related for MFs, so equity funds can hold them as part of the portfolio
The fund has become a real estate fund
The fund has stopped investing in equity
qs.why: REITs are equity-related for MFs from 2026. It is one holding among many, not a change of category.

title: Selling REITs and InvITs honestly: suitability and sizing
concept: Suitable for clients who understand market-linked units, can hold for several years and want a stream of rental or infrastructure income as part of a diversified plan.
Not suitable as a replacement for a fixed deposit, emergency money or money needed within a few years.
Size it as a small allocation. Do not let one REIT or InvIT dominate a client's portfolio.
Do not promise yields or call payouts 'guaranteed' or 'assured'. Do not compare a yield with a fixed deposit rate without explaining the difference.
Document why it suits the client: goal, horizon, risk profile and existing real estate or infrastructure exposure.

client.quote: "Can I put my retirement corpus in a REIT? The yield is better than my FD."
client.context: Retired client, 68, wants more income than his FD, low risk tolerance.

talk: "A REIT can fluctuate in price and its payouts can change. It cannot replace your safe money. If you want some exposure, we can keep it to a small share, and keep your income needs covered by safer products."

qs.prompt: A retired client with low risk tolerance wants to move his entire FD into a REIT for higher yield. What is the best advice?
options: Explain price and payout risk, keep essential income in safer products, and consider only a small allocation if suitable
Agree, since the yield is higher
Tell him REIT payouts are guaranteed
Suggest an InvIT instead, since it is safer
qs.why: Suitability and honesty come first. A REIT is market-linked and cannot replace safe, assured income.

qs.prompt: Which phrase is a compliance problem when selling a REIT?
options: "This REIT will assure you 8% a year."
"Let's check how much of your portfolio this should be."
qs.why: Promising a yield breaks fair-communication rules. Payouts and prices change.

qs.prompt: What is a sensible way to size a REIT or InvIT in a diversified portfolio?
options: A modest allocation sized to the client's goals, horizon and risk profile
The largest holding, because of the payout
qs.why: Concentration is a risk. Size it to fit the plan, and document why.

title: Time value of money: why ₹1 today beats ₹1 later
concept: Money today can be invested, so it is worth more than the same amount received later.
Present value (PV) is what a future amount is worth today. Future value (FV) is what today's money grows into.
FV = PV × (1 + r)^n, where r is the yearly rate and n is the number of years.
PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n. Discounting is just compounding in reverse.
A rate of return only means something when you also state the period it applies to.

client.quote: "I can get ₹10 lakh today or ₹12 lakh after three years. Which is better?"
client.context: Client weighing a lump sum now against a bigger payment later.

talk: "Let's put both on the same date. At 8% a year, ₹10 lakh today grows to about ₹12.6 lakh in three years, so ₹12 lakh later is worth less."
remember: Compare amounts on the same date.
State the rate and the period.

qs.prompt: ₹1,00,000 grows at 10% a year for 2 years. What is the future value?
qs.why: 1,00,000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = ₹1,21,000. Interest earns interest, so it is more than the ₹1,20,000 simple-interest answer.

qs.prompt: What does present value tell you?
options: What a future amount is worth in today's money
How much a fund will earn next year
The current NAV of a scheme
qs.why: Present value discounts a future amount back to today using a rate of return.

qs.prompt: A client is offered ₹1,00,000 today or ₹1,05,000 in one year. A safe deposit pays 8%. Which is worth more?
qs.why: ₹1,00,000 at 8% becomes ₹1,08,000 in a year, which beats ₹1,05,000.

title: Simple and compound growth, and the Rule of 72
concept: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount. Compound interest is paid on the original amount plus past interest.
The longer the period, the larger the gap between the two.
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual rate (in %). At 12%, about 6 years.
The rule is an approximation. It works best for rates between about 6% and 12%.
Compounding works against you too: loans and costs compound the same way.

client.quote: "How long will it take my money to double?"
client.context: Client asks for a quick mental-maths answer in the meeting.

talk: "Divide 72 by the return. At 8% it is about 9 years. At 12% about 6 years. It is a rough guide, not a promise of returns."

qs.prompt: Using the Rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 9% a year?
qs.why: 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years.

qs.prompt: ₹1,00,000 at 10% for 20 years. Roughly what is the compound value versus simple interest (₹3,00,000 in total)?
Why is the Rule of 72 not exact?
options: It is an approximation of the compounding formula
It only works for debt funds
qs.why: The exact doubling time is ln 2 ÷ ln(1+r). 72 is a handy approximation.

title: CAGR: one number for growth over years
concept: CAGR (compound annual growth rate) is the steady yearly rate that takes a starting value to an ending value.
CAGR = (End ÷ Start)^(1/years) − 1.
Absolute return ignores time: 100% over 3 years and 100% over 10 years look the same but are not.
CAGR smooths the ride. A fund can fall 30% in one year and still show a healthy 5-year CAGR.
Use CAGR for a single lump sum held for the whole period, not for SIPs (use XIRR).

client.quote: "This fund gave 150% in 7 years. Is that good?"
client.context: Client reads an absolute return on a pamphlet.

talk: "150% over 7 years is about 14.0% a year. Let's compare that with the benchmark and with a fixed deposit on the same dates."

qs.prompt: ₹1,00,000 becomes ₹2,00,000 in 5 years. What is the CAGR (nearest)?
qs.why: (2)^(1/5) − 1 = 14.87%. Not 20%, which is the simple average.

qs.prompt: Why is absolute return a weak way to compare funds?
options: It ignores how long the money was invested
qs.why: A 60% gain in 2 years is far better than 60% in 8 years. CAGR puts both on a yearly basis.

qs.prompt: A fund's value rises 20% in year 1 and falls 20% in year 2. What is the two-year result?
qs.why: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% loss. Averaging +20% and −20% to get 0% is a common mistake.

title: XIRR: returns when money goes in at different dates
concept: XIRR finds the annualised rate that fits every cash flow and its date: each SIP instalment, any withdrawal, and the final value.
Use XIRR for SIPs, STPs, top-ups and part-withdrawals. CAGR assumes one start and one end.
Each instalment has been invested for a different time, so a simple average of years is wrong.
Spreadsheets compute it: =XIRR(values, dates). Outflows are negative, the final value is positive.
Fund apps and factsheets usually show SIP returns as XIRR.

client.quote: "My SIP has run 3 years and shows 14%. Why does the fund show 11%?"
client.context: Client compares the fund's lump-sum CAGR with their own SIP XIRR.

talk: "The fund's 11% is a one-time investment for 3 years. Your SIP money went in month by month, so the later instalments had less time. The 14% is your personal XIRR."

qs.prompt: Which measure suits a monthly SIP that has run for 3 years?
qs.why: Cash flows happen on different dates, so XIRR is the right annualised measure.

qs.prompt: In an XIRR calculation, how are SIP instalments entered?
options: As negative amounts on their dates, with the current value as a positive amount
qs.why: Money you invest is an outflow (negative). The value today, or a withdrawal, is an inflow (positive).

qs.prompt: Why might a fund's 3-year CAGR differ from an investor's SIP XIRR?
options: Because the timing of instalments differs from a single lump sum
Because the fund changed its name
qs.why: CAGR is a one-date-in, one-date-out figure. SIP money enters at many dates.

title: SIP maths: how monthly investing builds a corpus
concept: A SIP invests a fixed amount at regular intervals. Each instalment compounds from its own date.
Future value of a monthly SIP ≈ P × [((1+i)^n − 1) ÷ i] × (1+i), where i is the monthly rate and n the number of months.
Example: ₹10,000 a month for 10 years at 12% a year (1% a month) grows to about ₹2,323,391, against ₹12,00,000 invested.
More than half the final amount is growth, but only if the market delivers the assumed rate. It is an illustration, not a forecast.
Starting earlier or raising the SIP yearly (a step-up) usually matters more than chasing a higher rate.

client.quote: "If I invest ₹10,000 a month for 10 years, how much will I get?"
client.context: Young client asking for a number to plan around.

talk: "At an assumed 12% a year, about ₹23 lakh on ₹12 lakh invested. Markets will not deliver 12% smoothly. Let's also see what 8% or 10% looks like so you plan for a range."
remember: Illustrate with a range of rates.

qs.prompt: ₹10,000 a month at 12% a year for 10 years gives about ₹23 lakh. How much of that is the investor's own money?
qs.why: 120 instalments × ₹10,000 = ₹12,00,000. The rest is assumed growth.

qs.prompt: What is the best way to present a SIP projection?
options: Show a range of assumed returns and say they are not guaranteed
Quote last year's return as the future rate
qs.why: Projections depend on an assumed rate. Use a range and say plainly that it is an illustration.

qs.prompt: Which change usually improves the final corpus most, other things equal?
options: Waiting for a market fall to start
Choosing a fund with a catchy name
qs.why: Compounding rewards time in the market. Delay is costly.

title: Inflation and real returns
concept: Inflation is the rise in prices over time. It reduces what each rupee can buy.
Real return ≈ (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1. A rough shortcut is nominal minus inflation.
A 7% return with 6% inflation gives a real return near 0.9%, not 1%.
Costs of education and healthcare can rise faster than headline inflation.
Goals should be written in today's money and then inflated to the date of need.

client.quote: "My FD gives 7%, which is safe. Why do you want to change it?"
client.context: Retired client keeping everything in fixed deposits.

talk: "At 6% inflation your 7% FD grows your buying power by less than 1% a year, before tax. We can look at how much you really need to grow by."
remember: Tax also reduces the real return.

qs.prompt: A deposit earns 8% a year and inflation is 6%. The exact real return is about:
qs.why: 1.08 ÷ 1.06 − 1 = 1.89%. Subtracting gives 2%, a close shortcut.

qs.prompt: A ₹50,000 monthly expense today at 6% inflation becomes about what in 10 years?
Why is looking only at the nominal return misleading?
options: Rising prices reduce what the returns can buy
qs.why: Real return shows the growth in purchasing power.

title: Goal maths: how much to invest each month
concept: Start with the goal in today's money, inflate it to the year it is needed, then work back to a monthly amount.
Inflate with the rate that fits the goal (education often rises faster than general prices).
Pick an assumed return to match the investment mix and the time. Short goals need lower, steadier assumptions.
Solve for the SIP: P = Target × i ÷ [((1+i)^n − 1) × (1+i)].
Review every year. Update for markets, income and goal changes.

client.quote: "I need ₹50 lakh for my daughter's college in 12 years. What SIP do I start?"
client.context: Parent with a clear goal and date.

talk: "Let's inflate the ₹50 lakh first. At 8% education inflation it is about ₹126 lakh in 12 years. Then we work out the monthly amount at a realistic return, and review it every year."

qs.prompt: A goal of ₹50 lakh in today's money, with 8% inflation for 12 years, becomes about:
What is the first step in goal-based SIP planning?
options: Define the goal amount in today's money and the date
qs.why: Everything else depends on the amount and the date.

qs.prompt: A client's goal is 2 years away. Which approach is most sensible?
options: Use a lower, steadier return assumption and avoid high-volatility assets
qs.why: Short horizons cannot ride out large falls. Keep the assumption and the risk low.

title: Risk numbers: volatility, drawdown and what they mean
concept: Standard deviation measures how much returns swing around their average. Higher means a bumpier ride.
Maximum drawdown is the largest fall from a peak to a trough. It shows the worst pain a holder felt.
Beta shows how much a fund moves compared with its benchmark. Beta above 1 means bigger swings than the market.
Sharpe ratio is return above the risk-free rate per unit of volatility. Higher is better, compared across similar funds only.
Risk numbers look backwards. They describe what happened, not what will.

client.quote: "Both funds gave 14%. Why do you say one is riskier?"
client.context: Client sees two funds with equal returns.

talk: "One fell 38% at its worst. The other fell 22%. Same return, different journey. The second may be easier to stick with."
remember: Return alone is half the story.

qs.prompt: What does maximum drawdown measure?
qs.why: It is the biggest decline an investor would have sat through.

qs.prompt: A fund has a beta of 1.3 against its benchmark. What does that suggest?
options: It tends to move more than the benchmark, both up and down
It moves half as much as the market
qs.why: Beta above 1 means amplified moves relative to the benchmark.

qs.prompt: Why should risk ratios like Sharpe be compared only across similar funds?
options: Different categories carry different risks and benchmarks
qs.why: A liquid fund and a small-cap fund cannot be judged on the same scale.

title: The cost of costs: how expense ratios compound
concept: Expense ratio is charged daily as a percentage of assets and is already reflected in NAV.
A small yearly difference compounds. 1% lower return for 20 years costs far more than 1% of the final amount.
Example: ₹10 lakh for 20 years at 12% becomes ₹96 lakh. At 11% it is ₹81 lakh. The 1% gap costs about ₹16 lakh.
Direct plans have lower expense ratios than regular plans because they carry no distributor commission.
Cost is one factor. A cheaper fund that underperforms still hurts. Explain what the client gets for the cost.

client.quote: "What is 1% extra cost? It's tiny."
client.context: Client comparing a regular plan with a direct plan.

talk: "On ₹10 lakh over 20 years, a 1% yearly cost difference is about ₹16 lakh. Small each year, big over time. Let me show you what my service adds for that cost."
remember: Be ready to explain value for cost.

qs.prompt: ₹10 lakh grows at 12% vs 11% for 20 years. Roughly what is the difference in the final amount?
Where is a fund's expense ratio deducted?
options: As a bill sent to the investor
qs.why: The NAV you see is already net of the running expenses.

qs.prompt: Which statement about cost is most balanced?
options: Cost matters, and so does what the advice and fund deliver for it
Only the cheapest fund is acceptable
qs.why: Be transparent about cost and clear about value.

title: Lumpsum or SIP, and the calculation mistakes to avoid
concept: A lump sum is fully invested from day one. A SIP spreads the entry over time.
Over long periods lumpsum often wins in rising markets because more money is invested for longer. SIP reduces the risk of a bad entry point.
SIPs help investors who earn monthly and who cannot time the market. They do not guarantee profit.
Common mistakes: averaging yearly returns, using CAGR for SIPs, ignoring costs and tax, quoting an assumed return as expected.
Always say the period, whether returns are annualised, and whether it is before or after tax.

client.quote: "Should I invest ₹12 lakh now or in 12 monthly instalments?"
client.context: Client received a bonus and fears a market fall.

talk: "If the market rises, the lump sum does better. If it falls soon, the instalments do better. I can't know which. The 12 instalments help you stay calm, which is also worth something."

qs.prompt: Which statement is accurate?
options: Lump sum can outperform in a steadily rising market; a SIP lowers the risk of a poorly timed entry
qs.why: Neither wins every time. They solve different problems.

qs.prompt: Returns for four years are +10%, +20%, −10% and +5%. What is wrong with saying the 'average return is 6.25%'?
options: The actual compound growth is lower than the simple average
It is too high by exactly 1%
qs.why: Compound growth for these four years is about 5.7% a year, lower than the 6.25% arithmetic mean.

qs.prompt: What should accompany any return number you quote to a client?
options: The period, whether it is annualised, and whether it is before or after tax
qs.why: Context makes the number usable and honest.

title: Bonds: coupon, price, face value and yield
concept: A bond is a loan. The issuer pays a fixed coupon (interest) and returns the face value on maturity.
Face value is the amount printed on the bond, often ₹100 or ₹1,000. Coupon rate × face value = coupon in rupees.
Price is what the bond trades for in the market today. It can be above, at or below face value.
Yield is the return an investor earns at today's price. Coupon is fixed, yield changes with the price.
Government securities (G-secs) carry sovereign credit. Corporate bonds carry the company's credit risk.

client.quote: "A bond gives a fixed rate, so there's no risk, right?"
client.context: Client who treats all fixed-income as guaranteed.

talk: "The coupon is fixed but the price in the market is not. If you sell before maturity the price can be lower or higher. And a company bond has the risk the company fails to pay."
remember: Coupon fixed; price and yield move.

qs.prompt: A bond has a face value of ₹100 and a 7% coupon. What coupon does it pay each year?
qs.why: 7% of ₹100 = ₹7 a year.

qs.prompt: Which statement about a bond's coupon and yield is correct?
options: Coupon is fixed at issue; yield changes as the price changes
Yield is fixed and coupon changes
qs.why: The coupon is a contract term. The yield reflects the price you pay.

qs.prompt: What extra risk does a corporate bond carry compared with a G-sec?
options: The risk the issuer cannot pay
qs.why: Credit risk is the risk of default or delay by the issuer.

title: Why bond prices fall when interest rates rise
concept: Existing bonds have fixed coupons. When new bonds offer higher rates, old bonds become less attractive, so their prices fall.
When rates fall, old higher-coupon bonds become more valuable, so prices rise.
The longer the bond has to maturity, the bigger the price move for the same change in rates.
If held to maturity, a bond pays face value, so interim price falls do not matter to the holder. A fund must show NAV daily, so the swing appears in NAV.
This is why debt funds can show negative returns over short periods.

client.quote: "Why did my debt fund go down? Debt funds are supposed to be safe."
client.context: Client sees a negative one-month return on a long-duration fund after a rate rise.

talk: "When market rates rise, the price of existing bonds drops. A fund holds many bonds and marks them each day, so the NAV dips. If rates stabilise the fund keeps earning the coupons."

qs.prompt: Market interest rates rise. What generally happens to the price of an existing bond?
qs.why: New bonds pay more, so older lower-coupon bonds must sell at a lower price to match.

qs.prompt: Which bond is likely to move more for the same rate change?
options: One with a longer time to maturity
qs.why: Longer-dated bonds are more sensitive to rate changes.

qs.prompt: Why can a debt fund's NAV fall even if no bond defaults?
options: Bond prices change with interest rates and the fund marks them daily
qs.why: NAV is based on daily market values, so rate-driven price moves flow into it.

title: Duration: how sensitive is the fund to rates?
concept: Modified duration estimates the % change in a bond's price for a 1% (100 bps) change in yield.
Price change ≈ − Modified duration × change in yield.
A fund with modified duration of 4 would fall about 4% if yields rose 1%, and rise about 4% if yields fell 1% (approximately, ignoring coupons).
Longer duration means more rate risk and, usually, more potential reward when rates fall.
Fund factsheets show average maturity, Macaulay duration, modified duration and yield to maturity (YTM).

client.quote: "What does duration of 6 years mean for my money?"
client.context: Client asks why a gilt fund's NAV moved so much.

talk: "Roughly, if yields rise 1%, a fund with duration of 6 could fall about 6% in price terms. The coupon income offsets some of that over time. Shorter duration funds move less."

qs.prompt: A fund has a modified duration of 3. If yields rise by 1%, the approximate effect on price is:
qs.why: Price change ≈ −3 × 1% = −3%, before counting the coupon income.

qs.prompt: Which fund is more sensitive to interest rate changes?
options: The one with the higher modified duration
The one with the lower duration
The one with the lower expense ratio
qs.why: Higher duration means a larger price swing for a given yield change.

qs.prompt: Where would you look to see a debt fund's modified duration?
options: The fund factsheet or portfolio disclosure
qs.why: Factsheets list duration, maturity and YTM.

title: Yield to maturity, accrual and mark-to-market
concept: Yield to maturity (YTM) is the annualised return if every bond in the portfolio is held to maturity and all payments are made as promised.
Accrual strategy: buy bonds and hold to maturity to earn the coupons. NAV rises steadily unless there are price shocks or defaults.
Duration strategy: the manager takes a view on rates and holds longer bonds if rates are expected to fall.
The portfolio YTM is a gross figure. Fund expenses and tax come out of it.
A high YTM can signal higher credit risk. It is not a free bonus.

client.quote: "The fund's YTM is 8%. So I will get 8%?"
client.context: Client reads YTM on a factsheet as a guaranteed return.

talk: "YTM is what the current portfolio would earn if held to maturity with no defaults, before expenses and tax. Your actual return can be different because prices change and the portfolio changes."
remember: Net of expenses and tax it is lower.
High YTM may mean higher risk.

qs.prompt: What does a fund's YTM represent?
options: The portfolio's expected annualised yield if held to maturity with all payments made
qs.why: YTM is a gross estimate based on today's holdings. It is not a promise.

qs.prompt: A debt fund shows YTM of 8% and expense ratio of 0.5%. What is a fair expectation?
options: Net return nearer 7.5% before tax, if nothing changes
qs.why: Expenses reduce the yield. Prices and the portfolio can also change.

qs.prompt: Why should a high YTM make you ask questions?
options: It may reflect lower-rated or less liquid bonds
It always means a good fund
It proves the manager is skilled
qs.why: Higher yields typically compensate for more risk.

title: Credit risk and ratings
concept: Credit risk is the chance that an issuer misses an interest or principal payment.
Rating agencies grade debt: AAA is highest, then AA, A, BBB, and so on. Below BBB is below investment grade.
Ratings can be cut (downgrade). Prices usually fall on a downgrade, before any default.
Higher-rated bonds pay lower yields. Lower-rated bonds pay more to compensate for the risk.
Diversification across issuers and sectors reduces, but does not remove, credit risk.

client.quote: "This fund shows 9% yield but my friend's shows 7.5%. Same category. Why?"
client.context: Client compares two corporate bond funds.

talk: "The 9% fund holds lower-rated papers. It earns more because it is taking more credit risk. If one issuer fails, the loss lands in NAV."

qs.prompt: Which rating indicates the strongest credit quality?
qs.why: AAA is the highest rating.

qs.prompt: What usually happens to a bond's price when the issuer is downgraded?
qs.why: A downgrade means higher perceived risk, so the market demands a higher yield and the price falls.

qs.prompt: Two funds are in the same category. One has a much higher yield. What should you check first?
options: The credit quality table of the portfolio
Which fund house has a bigger office
qs.why: Higher yield often comes from lower-rated paper.

title: The yield curve and what it says
concept: The yield curve plots yields against maturity: 3 months, 1 year, 5 years, 10 years.
A normal curve slopes upward: longer bonds yield more. A flat curve means little extra for lending longer. An inverted curve means short yields exceed long yields.
The slope shows market expectations for growth, inflation and policy rates.
Fund managers pick where on the curve to hold bonds. A steep curve rewards extending maturity.
The RBI repo rate mostly anchors the short end. The long end follows growth, inflation and supply of government bonds.

client.quote: "RBI cut rates. Should I buy a long-term debt fund?"
client.context: Client reacts to a headline.

talk: "A rate cut helps long-duration funds if the market has not priced it already. But if long-term yields do not fall, you may not gain. Duration is a bet on the path of rates, so size it carefully."

qs.prompt: What does an upward-sloping yield curve usually mean?
options: Short yields are higher than long
qs.why: A normal curve pays more for lending for longer.

qs.prompt: Which rate mainly influences the short end of the yield curve in India?
qs.why: The policy repo rate anchors overnight and short-term yields.

qs.prompt: Why is buying a long-duration fund after a rate cut headline not a sure win?
options: Markets may have already priced it in, and long yields depend on more than the repo rate
Long funds cannot gain from cuts
qs.why: Expectations move prices before the cut. Long yields also depend on inflation and supply.

title: SEBI's debt fund categories at a glance
concept: SEBI classifies debt funds mainly by portfolio duration, plus a few by credit rules.
Overnight: securities maturing in 1 day. Liquid: up to 91 days. Money market: up to 1 year. Ultra short: Macaulay duration 3–6 months. Low duration: 6–12 months.
Short duration: 1–3 years. Medium: 3–4 years. Medium to long: 4–7 years. Long duration: more than 7 years.

Gilt: at least 80% in government securities. Corporate bond: at least 80% in AA+ and above. Credit risk fund: at least 65% in AA and below. Banking and PSU: at least 80% in banks, PSUs and public financial institutions.
Dynamic bond and floater funds follow different rules. Always read the category and the scheme document.

client.quote: "Which debt fund category suits money I need in 6 months?"
client.context: Client has a goal inside a year.

talk: "For six months, we look at overnight, liquid or money market funds where the duration is short. A long-duration fund can swing in price within that time."
remember: Gilt = G-secs; credit risk = lower rated.

qs.prompt: Which category invests at least 80% in government securities?
qs.why: Gilt funds hold G-secs and carry sovereign credit, but still carry rate risk.

qs.prompt: A liquid fund invests in securities maturing within:
qs.why: SEBI defines liquid funds as holding securities with maturity up to 91 days.

qs.prompt: Which category has a minimum 65% allocation to AA-rated and below paper?
qs.why: Credit risk funds are designed to take more credit risk for higher yield.

title: Liquidity risk and what the 2020 episode taught
concept: Liquidity risk: not being able to sell a bond quickly without a big price cut.
In April 2020, a fund house wound up six debt schemes after redemptions overwhelmed lower-rated holdings. Investors were locked in for months.
Since then, SEBI has tightened rules on liquidity, valuation and disclosure for debt funds, and has allowed segregated portfolios (side pockets) when a bond is downgraded to default.
In a side pocket, the troubled bond is separated. Investors keep units in the main portfolio and in the side pocket; recoveries are paid out as they happen.
Open-ended funds promise daily liquidity. The assets must be able to support that promise.

client.quote: "Can I withdraw from a debt fund any day?"
client.context: Client assumes redemption is always instant.

talk: "Normally yes, and the money arrives in a day or two. In an extreme stress the fund can face limits. That is one reason we avoid putting emergency money in lower-rated funds."
remember: Side pocket separates a defaulted bond.

qs.prompt: What is a segregated portfolio (side pocket)?
options: A separate portfolio created to hold a defaulted or downgraded bond
qs.why: It lets the main portfolio continue while the troubled bond is handled separately.

qs.prompt: Why does liquidity risk matter for open-ended debt funds?
options: They promise daily redemption but hold bonds that may be hard to sell quickly
qs.why: A mismatch between redemption promises and asset liquidity creates stress.

qs.prompt: Which is the most suitable home for a client's emergency fund?
options: Overnight or liquid fund, or a savings account
qs.why: Emergency money needs stable value and quick access.

title: Taxation of debt funds
concept: Under rules in force since 1 April 2023, gains on specified debt-oriented mutual funds are taxed at the investor's slab rate, whatever the holding period. Indexation is not available.
Investors in the 30% slab therefore pay about 30% (plus surcharge and cess) on gains.
Fund-level distributions (IDCW) are taxed in the investor's hands at slab rates; TDS may apply above a limit.
Equity-oriented hybrids and arbitrage funds follow equity taxation rules, which differ.
Rules change by Budget. Check the current definition of a specified mutual fund and confirm with a CA.

client.quote: "Is a debt fund more tax-efficient than a fixed deposit?"
client.context: Client in the 30% slab compares tax on FD interest with a debt fund.

talk: "Today the gain is taxed at your slab rate in both cases. The difference is when you pay: an FD taxes you every year on interest, a debt fund only when you redeem. That deferral still has value, but it is not a rate advantage."

qs.prompt: How are gains from specified debt mutual funds taxed under rules in force from April 2023?
options: At the investor's slab rate, regardless of holding period
qs.why: The special long-term treatment and indexation were removed for these funds.

qs.prompt: What advantage does a debt fund still have over an FD for taxes?
options: Tax is payable only when units are redeemed, not every year
qs.why: Deferral of tax can help compounding, though the rate is the same.

qs.prompt: Why should you tell clients to confirm the latest tax rules with a CA?
qs.why: Tax law is amended often; advice must reflect the current position.

title: Matching debt funds to goals, and selling them honestly
concept: Match the fund's duration to the time the money is needed: days to months for overnight or liquid, 1–3 years for short duration, longer only if the client can ride out price swings.
Core idea: hold period should be at least the fund's duration so rate swings average out.
Use high-quality debt for stability. Use credit risk funds only for a small part, and only if the client understands the risk.
Never call a debt fund 'safe' or 'like an FD'. Say what can go wrong: rate moves, downgrade, default, liquidity.
Check the client's emergency fund, goals and tax slab before recommending.

client.quote: "I want something safer than equity that beats my savings account."
client.context: Client with money parked in a bank for 3 years, wants better returns.

talk: "For three years, a short-duration high-quality fund could fit. It can still show a small loss in a bad rate year, so I would keep the emergency money separate and only put in what you won't need for 3 years."

qs.prompt: A client needs money in about 4 months. Which category is most suitable?
qs.why: Short-duration, high-quality instruments suit short horizons.

qs.prompt: Which phrase is a communication problem when selling a debt fund?
options: 'It is as safe as an FD.'
'Match the period to the fund's duration.'
qs.why: Debt funds are market-linked and have no assured return.

qs.prompt: What is a sensible role for a credit risk fund in a portfolio?
options: A small satellite for investors who understand and accept credit risk
The core of an emergency fund
A replacement for a savings account
The main holding for a retired client
qs.why: Higher-yield, lower-quality paper is a risk asset and should be sized small.

title: PMS: a portfolio in your own name
concept: Portfolio Management Service (PMS) is a SEBI-registered service where a manager runs a portfolio of securities held in the client's own demat account.
SEBI rules set the minimum investment at ₹50 lakh per client.
Types: discretionary (manager decides), non-discretionary (client approves each trade) and advisory (manager advises, client executes).
Because securities sit in the client's name, there is no pooling: each client's portfolio and tax position can differ.
PMS providers must be registered with SEBI as portfolio managers. Check the registration before recommending.

client.quote: "What's the difference between a PMS and a mutual fund?"
client.context: HNI client with ₹1 crore considering a PMS.

talk: "In a mutual fund your money is pooled with others in one scheme. In a PMS the stocks are bought in your own demat account by the manager. Costs, taxes and risks are different, and the minimum is ₹50 lakh."

qs.prompt: What is the minimum investment per client in a PMS under SEBI rules?
qs.why: SEBI set the minimum PMS investment at ₹50 lakh.

qs.prompt: In a PMS, in whose name are the securities usually held?
qs.why: PMS portfolios are held directly by each client.

qs.prompt: In a discretionary PMS, who takes investment decisions?
qs.why: Discretionary means the manager decides within the agreed mandate.

title: PMS fees and reading the fine print
concept: Common structures: a fixed fee on assets, a performance fee above a hurdle, or a mix of both.
A hurdle rate is the return the manager must beat before earning a performance fee. A high-water mark means the fee applies only on gains above the previous peak.
Other charges can include brokerage, custody, exit load in the first years, and taxes on each trade.
Returns on marketing material may not match your actual returns: compare after-fee, after-cost figures.
Ask for the Disclosure Document, which sets out fees, risks and past performance in a standard form.

client.quote: "They charge only 20% of profits. That's cheap, no?"
client.context: Client sees a 'profit share only' PMS.

talk: "The structure matters: is there a hurdle? A high-water mark? What other fees apply? Let's compare what you would net after all costs with a similar mutual fund."

qs.prompt: What is a 'hurdle rate' in a PMS performance fee?
options: The minimum return the manager must beat before earning performance fees
qs.why: The manager earns the fee only on returns above the hurdle.

qs.prompt: What does a high-water mark do?
options: Charges performance fees only on gains above the previous peak value
qs.why: It prevents paying performance fees twice on the same gains after a fall.

qs.prompt: Where would you find a PMS's standardised description of fees, risks and performance?
qs.why: The Disclosure Document is the formal statement filed under SEBI rules.

title: AIFs: Category I, II and III
concept: Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are privately pooled funds regulated by SEBI, for sophisticated investors.
Minimum investment is generally ₹1 crore per investor. Angel funds have a lower threshold.
Category I: funds supporting the economy, such as venture capital, start-ups, infrastructure and social ventures.
Category II: funds that do not fall in I or III and do not use leverage beyond day-to-day needs, such as private equity and debt funds.
Category III: funds that use complex strategies and may use leverage or trade in derivatives, such as hedge funds and long-short funds.

client.quote: "My friend invested in a private equity fund. Can I?"
client.context: HNI client wants unlisted exposure.

talk: "That is usually an AIF. They need a larger ticket, often a lock-in of several years, and they are not as liquid as a mutual fund. Let's check if it suits your plan and your other liquid assets."
remember: Cat I, II, III by strategy and leverage.

qs.prompt: Which AIF category generally includes venture capital funds?
qs.why: Category I covers venture capital, start-ups, infrastructure and similar funds.

qs.prompt: Which category may use leverage and complex trading strategies?
qs.why: Category III funds such as hedge funds can use leverage and derivatives.

qs.prompt: Which is generally true about AIFs compared with mutual funds?
options: They have higher minimums and often longer lock-ins
They are for retail investors with ₹500
qs.why: AIFs are for larger investors and often have lock-ins.

title: Taxation of PMS and AIF in broad strokes
concept: PMS: each trade is taxed in the client's hands. Short-term gains on listed equity are taxed at 20% and long-term at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year (current rules; confirm). Trading activity can change treatment.
Cat I and Cat II AIFs are generally pass-through: income is taxed in investors' hands in the nature it arises, though business income stays with the fund.
Cat III AIFs are generally taxed at the fund level in many structures, so investors may see after-tax distributions.
TDS, GST on fees and securities transaction tax add to the cost layers.
Tax treatment depends on structure and facts. Always ask a CA before advising.

client.quote: "Which is more tax efficient, PMS or AIF?"
client.context: Client has a high tax slab.

talk: "It depends on the structure and what the fund actually earns. A PMS taxes each trade in your name. An AIF can pass income through or be taxed in the fund. We should look at this with your CA."
remember: PMS: taxed per trade in client's name.
Cat I/II pass-through; Cat III varies.

qs.prompt: In a PMS, who is taxed on the gains from trades?
options: The client, since the securities are in their name
qs.why: The investor holds the securities directly, so gains are taxed in the investor's hands.

qs.prompt: Which statement is generally true of Category I and II AIFs?
options: They are mostly pass-through for tax, with some income taxed at the fund level
They are taxed only on exit
qs.why: Pass-through status is a key feature, but exceptions apply, such as business income.

qs.prompt: Why should an advisor avoid saying one structure is 'more tax efficient' without details?
options: Treatment depends on structure, income type and the client's situation
Tax rules are the same everywhere
Taxes only matter for mutual funds
qs.why: Generalising can mislead. Use a CA for specifics.

title: PMS, AIF and mutual fund side by side
concept: Mutual fund: pooled, ticket from ₹100 or ₹500, daily NAV, high liquidity, strong disclosure, lower costs.
PMS: individually managed, min ₹50 lakh, holdings in client's name, more concentrated, fees vary, trade-level tax.
AIF: privately pooled, usually ₹1 crore minimum, may be illiquid, can invest in unlisted or complex strategies.
Higher cost and higher minimum must be justified by something a mutual fund cannot offer: access, customisation, strategy.
Clients with sizeable wealth often hold a mix, with mutual funds as the liquid core.

client.quote: "Is PMS better than mutual funds because it's for rich people?"
client.context: Client believes higher minimum means better returns.

talk: "A higher minimum does not mean higher returns. It means different structure, usually higher cost and more concentration. We should use it only if there is a reason, like a strategy you cannot get in a mutual fund."

qs.prompt: Which product offers daily NAV and the lowest minimum ticket?
qs.why: Mutual funds start from small amounts and publish a daily NAV.

qs.prompt: Which statement about higher minimums is correct?
options: They do not guarantee better returns
qs.why: Structure and strategy matter, not the size of the ticket.

qs.prompt: What should justify choosing a PMS or AIF over a mutual fund?
options: A specific strategy, access or customisation worth the extra cost and illiquidity
The ability to charge higher fees
qs.why: Each layer of cost and illiquidity must buy something clear.

title: SIF: the new middle ground
concept: Specialised Investment Funds (SIFs) were introduced by SEBI from 1 April 2025, between mutual funds and PMS/AIF.
They are run by mutual fund houses. The minimum investment is ₹10 lakh per investor, counted across a fund house's SIF strategies.
SIFs may use strategies that ordinary mutual funds cannot, such as limited short exposure through derivatives (long-short strategies).
The strategy names, limits and rules are set by SEBI. Read the scheme document carefully.
From 1 January 2026, REIT units count as equity-related instruments for SIFs as they do for mutual funds.

client.quote: "What is this new SIF? Is it a mutual fund?"
client.context: Client has seen SIF advertisements.

talk: "It is offered by mutual fund houses with a higher minimum of ₹10 lakh and a wider set of strategies, including limited shorting. It is more complex than a regular fund and can swing more."

qs.prompt: What is the minimum investment in a SIF per investor under SEBI's framework?
qs.why: SEBI set a ₹10 lakh threshold, counted across a fund house's SIF strategies.

qs.prompt: Who manages SIFs?
qs.why: SIFs are launched by SEBI-registered asset management companies.

qs.prompt: Which feature can a SIF have that a regular equity mutual fund generally cannot?
qs.why: SIF strategies allow long-short positions within limits.

title: Who these products suit, and who they do not
concept: Suitable for clients who already have a solid core of liquid investments, adequate insurance and emergency funds.
Look for the ability to take higher risk, to lock in money for years, and to understand strategy.
Not suitable for money needed soon, for first-time investors, or for those who cannot tolerate large swings.
Concentration risk: a PMS may hold 15–25 stocks. One bad bet is more visible.
Document the reasons. Suitability is judged by the client's profile, not the product's brochure.

client.quote: "I have ₹60 lakh and it's all I have. Should I put ₹50 lakh in a PMS?"
client.context: Client keen on a PMS but with no other savings.

talk: "That would put almost everything in one concentrated product with fees and no easy exit. A smaller allocation after building your emergency fund and core holdings is safer."

qs.prompt: A client has ₹60 lakh in total savings, no emergency fund. What is the best advice on putting ₹50 lakh in a PMS?
options: Do not; build the core and an emergency fund first and allocate only a suitable portion
Do it, since the minimum is ₹50 lakh
Do it, because PMS returns are higher
qs.why: The product would dominate the client's wealth with little liquidity.

qs.prompt: Which client profile best fits an AIF or PMS?
options: An investor with surplus wealth, a long horizon and high risk capacity
A retired person needing monthly cash
qs.why: These products need capacity to absorb risk and illiquidity.

qs.prompt: Why is concentration an important PMS risk?
options: Portfolios often hold few stocks, so single-stock outcomes matter more
qs.why: Fewer holdings amplify gains and losses.

title: Reading a track record without being fooled
concept: Ask whether returns are time-weighted or money-weighted, gross or net of fees, and for what period.
Compare with the right benchmark and over the same period. A PMS can look good if the benchmark is mismatched.
Check consistency: many years, not one lucky year. Look at the worst fall, not only the best year.
Beware survivorship: closed or merged products vanish from the lists, leaving only winners.
Ask for performance of the strategy, not just 'the best client account'.

client.quote: "This PMS did 28% last year. Isn't that great?"
client.context: Client reacts to one standout year.

talk: "One year can be luck. Let's see 5 years net of fees, versus an index and a similar mutual fund, and how deep the worst fall was."

qs.prompt: Which return figure is most useful when comparing a PMS with an index?
options: Net-of-fee returns over the same long period
Gross return in the best year
qs.why: After-fee, like-for-like figures show what the client really keeps.

qs.prompt: What is survivorship bias?
options: Looking only at products that survived, which hides the failed ones
qs.why: Failed or closed products drop out, making the group look better than it was.

qs.prompt: Why look at drawdown as well as returns?
options: To see the worst fall the investor had to sit through
qs.why: Drawdown shows the real risk experienced.

title: Red flags: when it's not what it seems
concept: Guaranteed or assured returns on a PMS or AIF are a warning sign. These are market-linked products.
Unregistered 'portfolio managers' or advisors: verify registration on SEBI's website before dealing.
Pressure to invest quickly, or claims of 'inside' information, or returns that look too steady.
Complex, hidden or unusually high fees; refusal to share the Disclosure Document or Private Placement Memorandum.
Report suspicious offers to SEBI's complaint system (SCORES) and the exchange.

client.quote: "This person promises 3% a month, with documents. Seems real."
client.context: Client shows you a forwarded WhatsApp pitch.

talk: "Nobody can promise returns on a market product. Steady monthly returns are a classic sign of trouble. Let's check his SEBI registration before sending a rupee."

qs.prompt: An agent promises a fixed 3% a month from a 'PMS'. What is the correct response?
options: Treat it as a red flag, check SEBI registration, and do not invest
Invest a small amount to test
qs.why: Guaranteed market returns are not legitimate.

qs.prompt: Where can you verify whether a portfolio manager is registered?
qs.why: SEBI maintains the list of registered portfolio managers and advisors.

qs.prompt: Which is an acceptable approach for an advisor who suspects a scam product?
options: Warn the client and report it through SEBI's complaint system
Quietly sell it with a commission
qs.why: Protecting clients and reporting fraud is part of professional duty.

title: Selling PMS, AIF and SIF responsibly
concept: Start with suitability: goal, horizon, liquidity, existing portfolio, risk capacity and experience.
Share the Disclosure Document or PPM and walk through fees, lock-ins, risks and exit terms in plain words.
Do not promise or imply returns. Do not compare gross figures of one product with net figures of another.
Disclose conflicts of interest, such as commissions or distribution fees.
Size it as a satellite. Revisit every year: has the strategy, the team or the client's situation changed?

client.quote: "Just tell me, will this beat my mutual funds?"
client.context: Client wants a yes or no.

talk: "I can't promise that. What I can say is how it is built, what it costs, how it has done across different markets, and why it may fit a small part of your portfolio."

qs.prompt: Which step must come first when recommending a PMS or AIF?
options: Understand the client's goals, horizon, liquidity and risk capacity
qs.why: Suitability drives the recommendation.

qs.prompt: What should an advisor say when a client asks, 'Will this beat my mutual funds?'
options: That no one can promise it, and explain structure, costs, history and fit
Yes, by at least 5% a year
qs.why: Honest framing avoids implied promises.

qs.prompt: What does disclosing a conflict of interest mean here?
options: Telling the client about commissions or fees you earn on the product
qs.why: Transparency about incentives lets the client weigh the advice.

title: Capital gains on mutual funds: the basics
concept: Equity-oriented funds hold at least 65% in equity. Gains within 12 months are short-term (20%). After 12 months, long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year are taxed at 12.5% (rates under current rules; confirm each year).
Specified debt-oriented funds: gains taxed at the investor's slab rate regardless of holding period (see debt course).
Other funds (for example equity 35–65%): long-term if held more than 24 months, taxed at 12.5% without indexation; shorter holds are taxed at slab rate.
Cess and surcharge are added on top. The tax is on gains only, not on the amount redeemed.
Gain = redemption value − cost of units sold, matched on a first-in-first-out basis.

client.quote: "If I redeem ₹10 lakh from my equity fund, do I pay tax on all ₹10 lakh?"
client.context: Client fears the tax on the whole amount.

talk: "No, only on the gain. If ₹5 lakh of that is long-term gain, the first ₹1.25 lakh in the year is exempt and the remaining ₹3.75 lakh is taxed at 12.5%, about ₹46,875 plus cess. Let's confirm with your CA."

title: FIFO, tax lots and the cost of switching
concept: Units are redeemed on a first-in-first-out basis: the oldest units are treated as sold first.
A switch from one scheme to another is a redemption plus a fresh purchase. It can trigger tax and exit load.
Switching between plans of the same scheme (regular to direct) is also treated as a transfer, so tax and load may apply.
Exit load is a charge for leaving early. Check the period; it applies to the amount redeemed or switched.
Before switching, compare the cost (tax + load) with the benefit of the new fund.

client.quote: "I want to move to a better fund. Just switch it, right?"
client.context: Client wants to move ₹8 lakh from an underperformer.

talk: "A switch counts as a sale and a new purchase. We pay tax on gains and maybe an exit load. Let's see if the better fund is likely to earn that back, and time the move to minimise tax."

qs.prompt: What does a switch from one mutual fund scheme to another amount to for tax purposes?
options: A redemption followed by a purchase
qs.why: Switches are treated as a sale of units and a new purchase.

qs.why: First-in-first-out matches the earliest purchases first.

options: The load may apply on units redeemed before the exit period ends
Exit load is a tax refund
Exit load applies to all SIPs after a year
It is charged only on debt

title: Tax harvesting: using the ₹1.25 lakh exemption
concept: Long-term capital gains on listed equity and equity-oriented funds are exempt up to ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year (current rules).
Harvesting means selling and re-buying units to realise gains within the exemption. It resets the cost price higher.
The benefit: lower future tax. The costs: exit loads, transaction costs and the risk of being out of the market for a day.
Use it as a year-end routine for clients who have large long-term holdings and stay within the limit.
Do not harvest if the savings are small compared with costs, and remember short-term gains are taxed at a higher rate.

client.quote: "My fund has gone up a lot. How can I reduce tax later?"
client.context: Client with ₹3 lakh unrealised long-term gains.

talk: "Each year the first ₹1.25 lakh of long-term gains is exempt. If we realise that much and reinvest, your cost goes up and less of the gain is taxed later. We need to check exit loads and fees before doing it."

qs.prompt: What is the main purpose of tax harvesting?
options: To realise gains within the annual exemption so the cost basis resets higher
qs.why: Harvesting uses the yearly exemption to reduce future taxable gains.

qs.prompt: Which factor can reduce or cancel the benefit of harvesting?
qs.why: Costs can outweigh the tax saved.

qs.prompt: When is harvesting least sensible?
options: When the gains are small and costs exceed the tax saved
When the gains are above the exemption
When the fund has a nil exit load
qs.why: Compare the tax saving with the cost before acting.

title: IDCW, TDS and what shows up on a tax statement
concept: IDCW (income distribution cum capital withdrawal) is the current name for dividend payouts from mutual funds.
IDCW is taxed in the investor's hands at slab rates. TDS may be deducted when payouts cross a threshold in a year.
Growth plans have no payouts, so there is no tax until units are sold.
Capital gains statements from RTAs (CAMS, KFintech) and the AMCs list each redemption, holding period and gain.
Keep these and the annual tax statement to file returns correctly. Mismatches with AIS/26AS can trigger notices.

client.quote: "Why did I get a tax statement when I didn't sell anything?"

talk: "IDCW payouts count as income for the year, taxed at your slab. A growth option gives no payouts, so tax applies only when you sell. Let's see whether growth suits you better."

qs.why: There is no income to tax until a sale.

title: Old versus new tax regime, and where ELSS fits
concept: Individuals can choose between the new tax regime (lower slab rates, fewer deductions) and the old regime (higher rates, deductions such as Section 80C).
Section 80C allows up to ₹1.5 lakh in deductions in the old regime, including ELSS, PPF, EPF and life insurance premiums.
ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme) has a 3-year lock-in, the shortest among 80C options.
Under the new regime, ELSS gives no deduction. It is simply an equity fund with a lock-in.
The better regime depends on income and deductions. Calculate both each year; regime rules change with Budgets.

talk: "ELSS saves tax only in the old regime. If you are in the new regime, an ordinary diversified equity fund without a lock-in is often more flexible. Let's check which regime is cheaper for you first."

qs.why: ELSS has a 3-year lock-in.

title: Retirement planning: the shape of the problem
concept: Retirement has two phases: building a corpus (accumulation) and living off it (decumulation).
Key unknowns: how long you live, inflation, returns and sequence of returns, health costs.
Start with expenses in today's money, inflate them to retirement date, and plan for 25–35 years afterwards.
Sources of income: EPF/NPS, pension, annuity, rent, interest, withdrawals from mutual funds.
Plan for the surviving spouse, and for a buffer for medical costs.

Using 25 times the first year expense, the corpus is about ₹7.7 crore. At a 3.5% withdrawal it would be ₹8.8 crore.
Then work back to the monthly SIP required using the goal maths from the foundation course.
These are planning aids, not guarantees. Review every year.

talk: "The number looks big because inflation is big over 25 years. We can bring it down by retiring later, spending less, adding other income, or starting higher. Let's test each lever."

qs.why: Annual expense ÷ 0.04 = 25 × annual expense = ₹7.7 crore.

qs.why: A lower withdrawal rate needs a larger corpus.

qs.why: Assuming unrealistic returns is not a plan.

title: Withdrawing: SWP, buckets and sequence risk
concept: A Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) pays a fixed amount from a fund each month. Units are redeemed, so each withdrawal has a capital gain part.
Sequence-of-returns risk: poor returns early in retirement hurt more than poor returns later, because withdrawals shrink the corpus when it is low.
Bucket strategy: hold 2–3 years of expenses in safe, liquid funds, the next 5 years in debt or hybrid, and the rest in equity for growth.
Refill the safe bucket from the growth bucket in good years. This avoids selling equity in a crash.
Review the withdrawal rate each year. Be ready to trim spending in a bad year.

client.quote: "What if the market falls right after I retire?"
client.context: Pre-retiree anxious about timing.

talk: "That is exactly what the buckets are for. Your next 2–3 years of expenses sit in safe funds, so you don't have to sell equity at a low. We refill the bucket in better years."

qs.prompt: What is sequence-of-returns risk?
options: Poor returns early in retirement damaging the corpus more because withdrawals continue
Buying funds in the wrong order
qs.why: Early losses combined with withdrawals shrink the base that has to recover.

qs.why: It covers near-term expenses so equity need not be sold in a downturn.

options: Each redemption has a gain portion that is taxed as per the fund's rules

title: EPF, PPF and NPS: the retirement building blocks
concept: EPF: for salaried employees, employee and employer contributions earn a notified interest rate; withdrawals have conditions.
PPF: 15-year government-backed scheme with a yearly deposit limit, and interest rate reset by the government each quarter.
NPS: market-linked pension account with equity, corporate bond and government bond choices; contributions to Tier I are locked until retirement age with partial withdrawals allowed in specific cases.
At NPS exit, part of the corpus must buy an annuity and the rest can be taken as a lump sum; the rules have been updated several times, so check the latest.
These schemes cover the safe and tax-advantaged portion; mutual funds add flexibility and growth.

client.quote: "I already have EPF and PPF. Do I need more?"
client.context: Client with some safe retirement savings.

talk: "They are a solid base, but their returns may not beat inflation by much over 25 years. We can estimate whether they cover your needs and add growth assets for the gap."

qs.prompt: Which of these is a government-backed small savings scheme with a 15-year tenure?
qs.why: PPF has a 15-year term.

qs.prompt: What is true about NPS?
options: It is a market-linked pension product with restrictions on withdrawals
qs.why: NPS invests in market assets and has exit rules tied to retirement.

qs.prompt: Why might EPF and PPF alone fall short for a long retirement?
options: Their returns may not comfortably beat inflation over decades
qs.why: Safe schemes offer stability but limited growth.

title: The advisor's role: goals, documents and humility
concept: Begin with the client's goals, ages, dependants, health, income, assets and liabilities.
Build a written plan with assumptions: inflation, returns, retirement age, longevity. Show a base case and a bad case.
Separate tax advice from investment advice where needed, and involve a CA for tax filing and structure.
Revisit the plan annually and after life events: job change, child, inheritance, illness.
Do not promise outcomes. Say what is assumed, what is not in your control, and what the client can change.

client.quote: "Just tell me if I will be fine at 60."
client.context: Client wants certainty.

talk: "I can show you where you are on track and what changes the result most. Nobody can promise the future, but we can build a plan that holds up in a bad case and review it every year."
remember: Written plan, base and bad case.

qs.prompt: What should a written retirement plan include?
options: Assumptions, a base case and a stress case
qs.why: Showing a bad case builds a more robust plan.

qs.prompt: When should an advisor involve a CA?
options: For tax structure, filing and complex tax questions
Only if the fund has fallen
qs.why: Tax is a specialist area; collaboration protects the client.

qs.prompt: Which life event should trigger a plan review?
options: A job change, an inheritance or an illness
qs.why: Major changes alter the assumptions behind the plan.
